Tiny Orchestral Metronome
questions  |  answers  |  history
◀  Back to the Metronome

This page explains functionality of the Tiny Orchestral Metronome. Assume nothing. If you've never used a metronome before, suggestion: begin here and skim all topics. If you already know what a metronome is and you want to understand the Accelerator, the Practice Log, or History Sync, you can jump directly to each section.

The short version: this is a metronome that invites the universe to set your beginning tempo, accelerates upward over a fixed number of minutes, and keeps a record of every minute you practice, including what you practiced. It runs in a web browser on any device you own, and your practice history follows you between devices if you log in with a free Github account.

01

History

What is this and where did it come from?

It began as a practice tool built to deliver what I wish existed in one Metronome. I built it for my own needs as a daily practicing musician. It does what it does based on my needs evolved over 40 years of practice. This is not what a product development committee would have asked for. Key Features: a rotary dial you can drag with your thumb. Three tones: woodblock, bar chime, and cowbell. A tuning reference. All designed to keep you focused on intentional practice.

The first working version was completed in March 2026, and the intent then was modest: get the dial, the sounds, the tuning tone, and the tempo range behaving properly on a phone. Timing on a phone is harder than it sounds, and most of that first stretch went into building a rock solid playback engine. The version you are using now is what became possible once that groundwork was completed. With the timing reliable, the tempo automation and practice tracking could be built on top of it.

Why not simply use one of the hundreds of existing metronome apps?

Because none of them do the three things that matter together. Most metronomes keep a tempo. A few will ramp a tempo. Almost none will deliver a tempo you did not choose, and almost none will quietly record what you actually do and share a record of your work one month later. Those three ideas belong in one instrument, and putting them together here is the whole point.

What does the version number mean?

Every release is numbered and the number appears in three places: the browser tab title, a small gray line under the dial, and the copyright line at the bottom of the page. Quoting that number is the fastest way to discover and describe a problem. If you discover a problem (or have a feature idea) this version number tells me exactly which build you were using when you share your feedback.

02

The metronome itself

What is a metronome for?

A metronome makes a sound at an exact and unchanging interval. You play along with it. Where you play early or late against this sound reveals something to work on. Developing reliable timing and Speed is an obvious use and, perhaps, the least interesting one. The real work is in developing reliability and accuracy across a full range of tempos.

The interval is measured in beats per minute, written BPM. At 60 BPM you hear one click every second. At 120 BPM you hear two clicks every second. Mostly obvious. 

How do I set the tempo?

Drag the dial. Put a finger or the mouse on the round face and move it in a circle, the same motion as a hardware tempo wheel. The number in the panel below tracks your finger. On a keyboard, the up and down arrows step one setting at a time, which is the accurate way to land on an exact number.

The range runs from 40 to 232 BPM across 42 settings. Those settings are not evenly spaced. They follow the traditional metronome sequence, which is fine-grained at slow tempos where small changes are audible and coarse at fast ones where they are not. All changes are in 4 BPM increments (by design). Would you prefer to be able to dial in a specific, arbitrary BPM? Let me know. That is feasible.

The dial. Drag the face. The knot at the center is the Guitar Craft knot.

What is the word under the BPM number?

That is the Italian tempo name for the range you are in. Adagio, Moderato, Allegro and the rest. It is the vocabulary printed on written music for the last few centuries, and it updates as you turn the dial. It is there for orientation and it changes nothing about the sound.

120 BPM, with the tempo name for that range underneath.

How do I make it play?

Press BEGIN. The button is green while the metronome is silent, because green means GO. Once it is running the same button turns red and reads STOP. The space bar does the same job if you have a keyboard.

The first press is also doing invisible work. Browsers refuse to make any sound until a human has touched the page, which is a rule that exists to stop websites shouting at you unprompted. That first press is what unlocks audio, so on some devices the first beat lands a fraction later than the ones that follow.

Green means go. Running, the same button turns red and reads STOP.

What is the counter in the middle of the dial?

How long you have held this tempo. It appears when you press Begin, counts up from zero, and sits over the knot so you can read it without looking anywhere else. Under an hour it reads minutes and seconds, and past an hour it adds the hours.

It counts a run at one tempo, which is not the same thing as a session. Move the dial and the count ends and a new one begins from zero, because you are now holding a different tempo and the old number no longer describes anything. Press Stop and it freezes on the time you reached, dimmed, and stays there until you begin again. The Accelerator ends it too, since moving the tempo is the whole point of the Accelerator and the count would otherwise restart every few seconds.

Changing the BEAT or changing the sound leaves it running. Those change what you hear on a beat, not the tempo you are holding.

What is the BEAT row, and why does it skip from 0 to 2?

It sets how many beats make a bar, and it accents the first one. Choose 4 and every fourth click becomes a different sound, which tells your ear where the bar begins without needing to count. Choose 3 for a waltz, 5 or 7 for odd meters. Zero means no accent at all, every click identical, and zero is where the metronome begins.

There is no 1 because a bar of one beat has nothing to accent against, which is the same thing as zero.

Choosing a number also reveals a second sound row, marked First Beat, and it sits above the other one because that is the order you hear them in. First Beat is the sound the downbeat uses and Other Beats is the sound the rest of the bar uses, so you can put a cowbell on the 1 and a woodblock on the rest. With the Beat row on zero there is no downbeat, so the First Beat row is not shown and the remaining row reads All Beats, which is what it governs.

The two rows are always held to different sounds while a meter is chosen. Loudness alone is not enough to mark a bar. A listener who cannot clearly find the 1 supplies their own grouping instead, and five even beats get heard as two-plus-three, so the downbeat needs its own voice rather than the same voice slightly louder. Pick a sound already in use in the other row and that other row steps aside: whichever one you just touched maintains your choice.

Beats to the bar. The first beat of each bar is accented.

What are Wood, Bar and Cowbell?

Those are the three voices. Wood is a dry woodblock sound, short and percussive, and it cuts through a loud instrument. Bar is a pitched chime with a longer tail, and it sits better under quiet playing. Cowbell is the loudest and the most stubborn, and it plows through. Pick whichever one you stop noticing, because a click you have tuned out is a click you are no longer listening to. Or playing with. 

All three are leveled against each other, which matters more than it sounds. The differentiation is in the timbre of each sound, their relative levels are the same (by design). 

Three voices. On zero this row reads All Beats. Choose a meter and a First Beat row appears above it.

What does PITCH do?

It plays a steady reference tone so you can tune. The six buttons are 440 through 445 Hz. A440 means the A above middle C vibrating 440 times a second, and it is the pitch most of the world tunes to. The higher options exist because some orchestras and some ensembles tune deliberately sharp of 440, and because a guitar tuned a hair sharp of a room tuned to 440 will sound bright rather than flat. Press a button, tune to what you hear, press it again to silence it.

Six reference tones, 440 through 445 Hz.

The volume slider does not change my phone volume. Why?

That slider controls this instrument only. It sits inside the audio path of the metronome itself, ahead of the output, so it scales the click and nothing else. Your ringer, your music, and your hardware volume keys are untouched. Use the slider to balance the click against your instrument, and the hardware keys to set how loud the whole device is.

This slider moves the click only. It never touches system volume.
03

Spin the Metronome

What does the Spin button do?

It invites the universe to set your beginning tempo, and then plays it. Press it and the dial accelerates, slows, and lands, and the metronome begins at whatever it landed on. That happens whether or not the metronome was running when you pressed it, so a Spin is one gesture rather than two. Where it lands is where you begin, and it will be an appropriate tempo for the moment you are actually in rather than one where you always begin by default. Or habit.

Why would I want a tempo I did not choose?

Because your own (default) choice may be a rut. Given a free hand, every player returns to the same two or three tempos, and those are the tempos where what you practice already feels comfortable. Comfortable is where practice stops being useful. A tempo arriving from outside invites you to visit a tempo you would not have chosen, and somewhere you would not have chosen is exactly where new, useful information resides.

Nothing here is random. The spin is an invitation, and the tempo that answers it is the appropriate one for this particular moment. Your part is to accept it and begin. There is nothing to negotiate and nothing to argue with, and that is most of the value.

One press. The universe sets the tempo.

Can I overrule it?

Yes, and the value comes from not doing so. Of course, the dial still works after the spin and the arrows still step. Spin again if you like, though a second spin is usually you negotiating. Accepting what you were given is the discipline, but this software does not enforce it. You are always in control. 

Does the spin set the Accelerator too?

The spin sets the metronome tempo. The Accelerator keeps its own beginning tempo, target tempo, and duration, and you set those separately. A common way to work is to spin for a warm-up (especially with a group), play with it for awhile (15m recommended), then open the Accelerator and build a session around what you observed.

04

The Accelerator

What is the Accelerator?

It raises the tempo for you, in steps, over a length of time you set. You give it a beginning tempo, a target tempo, a duration in minutes, and a step size in BPM. It works out how long to hold each tempo so that the whole climb fits the duration, then it runs. You keep playing. It does the arithmetic and the moving.

An example. Beginning tempo 120, target tempo 160, duration 15 minutes, increase by 4. That is ten steps of 4 BPM, so it holds each tempo for roughly a minute and a half, and after fifteen minutes you are playing at 160 having never once reached for the dial.

The four numbers that define a climb, with the estimate underneath.

Why is that better than turning the dial myself?

Two reasons. First, every time you touch the dial you stop playing, and the stopping is expensive. And a distraction. Second: when you control the tempo you cheat. You linger at the tempo that feels good and you skip past the one that exposes a limit. Or a problem. The Accelerator does not care how you feel about 138 BPM. It arrives there on schedule and it stays for its allotted time. And then it gets faster. The Accelerator enables you to find and track your limits over time. Ex. does my right hand always tense up and freeze when I reach 96 BPM?  Is my upper limit increasing over time? Or changing day to day, hour to hour? 

What are the Quick Presets?

Three ready-made climbs from 120 to 232. Express covers it in 5 minutes, Standard in 15, Extended in 30. These exist because setting four numbers before every session can be a form of friction, and friction is what stops us from practicing. Press one and press Begin Accelerator. Adjust the four rows underneath whenever a preset is not what you want. These are the timeframes I most use when practicing intentionally. I decide how long I have to practice (before my flight begins boarding, late at night before bed. first thing in the morning before coffee or sitting. Then: the metronome manages my time and tempo so I can relax into a rhythm. And grow with it over time. 

Express, Standard, Extended. All three climb 120 to 232.

What do Bars Left and Time Left mean?

Bars Left counts the bars remaining at the tempo you are playing now. Time Left counts the minutes remaining in the whole session. Between them you always know both how long until the next change and how long until the session completes.

Bars matter more than seconds to a musician. Knowing you have six bars left tells you where to place the phrase you are in the middle of. Knowing you have nine seconds left tells you nothing you can use.

Why is there a smaller number beside the live BPM?

That is the half-tempo. At 152 BPM it reads 76. A great deal of practice happens against the half, either because the material is felt in half time or because the half is where you check whether the fast version is genuinely in time or merely fast. Having the number visible saves my brain power so I can see the divided number without thinking too hard, or doing math while I'm practicing.

The live tempo, with the half beside it.

What happens when the session completes?

The Accelerator reaches the target tempo, holds there, and keeps playing. Nothing stops. Everything from that point forward is logged separately as Play Time. Press End Session when you are done, and the session is written to the log.

The climb drawn out. The cursor moves along it as you play.
05

Play Time

What is Play Time and why is it counted separately?

Play Time is every minute you kept playing after the Accelerator reached its target. It is counted apart from the session because it means something different. The session is the work you committed to. The Play Time is the work you did not have to do, and it is the most interesting number on the page.

Keeping them separate also protects the session length. A 15-minute session that ran 40 minutes is still a 15-minute session with 25 minutes of play attached, which is a more useful record than a 40-minute session that no longer resembles what you set out to do.

Where does it show up?

Inside the Practice Log, on its own strip, with totals for today, this week, and all time. There is also a small live badge in the Accelerator panel while you are playing, so you can watch it accumulate.

What are the 'cards' that appear while I play?

Practice quotes. A card rises at the foot of the screen every few minutes while the transport is running, carrying one line from a collection of aphorisms, quotations and lyrics, attributed and where possible linked to its source. They are there to be read as inspiration in passing rather than studied, and they arrive on playing time only, so a card never appears while the instrument is sitting idle.

Each quote is shown once before any repeats. The counter beneath the switch tells you how far through the collection you are, and how many complete passes you have made.

Can I move through the quotes myself?

Yes. The card carries a back and a forward control alongside its dismiss button. Forward brings the next line straight away rather than waiting for it. Back returns to the card before it, and keeps returning, so a line you half read as it faded is still there. Walk back several and go forward again and you pass through those same lines in order before a new one is drawn.

Moving deliberately restarts the card's own clock, so a line you asked for stays long enough to read. The back control hides itself when there is nothing behind you. I recommend NOT scrolling through the quotes, and I prefer to have them become subtle, frequent surprises that offer energy and insights while you're focused on practicing. 

06

Practice Categories

What is a category?

A category is a name you invent for one kind of work. Scales. Repertoire. Sight reading. The third movement. Whatever divisions describe how you actually spend your time. Each one carries a color, and the color is what you see later on the calendar.

One practiced day among empty ones. Four categories, four wedges.

How do I make one?

Open the Practice Log, find Practice Categories, press Add, pick a color, type a name. Once a category exists it appears in the Practicing row inside the Accelerator, and you choose one there before you begin. Choose it before, not after, because after the session you will not remember and you will not bother.

Choose the category before you press Begin.

What are the eight categories that came with it?

They are mine, and they are what I am working on this year. They are there so the app is not empty on the first day and so you can see what a real set looks like. Delete all eight and put in your own. I would rather you did.

Three of them are mechanics. right-hand is my classic right-hand-only warm up. I use it every day to find where my center of gravity is for right-hand speed that morning. all or nothing is symmetrical scale work for the left hand, stretching between the second and third fingers. A whole step between 2 and 3 is one of my weakest attributes and this builds strength and independence there. hammer on is work from the past year, designed to build equal strength in each finger.

The rest is repertoire. discipline is Discipline, the King Crimson piece, and there are Guitar Craft versions of it too. I cycle through the whole piece under acceleration, to keep driving up my average viable speed on all the parts. moving is The Moving Force, mostly an anchor exercise for my third and fourth fingers while I work on four-string right-hand arpeggios. driving is the The Driving Force melody, tone first, then speed and flow.

Two are pieces I am still learning. bach is Jesu, Joy of Man's Desiring, where I am working on hybrid picking and on sustain in a piece driven by counterpoint. paganini is my ongoing work to memorize and execute the Moto Perpetuo.

Why bother naming things?

Because the total is not the interesting number. Nine hours this month is a fact with no consequence. Seven of those nine hours on scales and forty minutes on repertoire is a diagnosis, and it tells you what to change next week. Categories turn a number you cannot act on into one you can.

What if I do not choose a category?

Every minute you run the metronome is tracked, whether you choose anything or not. Press Begin, or press Spin, and play. The session lands in the log under practice, which is the built-in category the metronome uses when you have not picked another one. It shows on the calendar in pale blue like any other, it counts toward your totals, and it builds your streak.

Nothing has to be set up first. No account, no sync, no GitHub. Turn on the metronome and the record begins.

Choosing a category is how you make that record worth reading later, and you can also tag a session afterwards from the log if you did not choose one before you began.

07

The Practice Log

What does the log record?

Every completed session, with its date, its length, the tempos it covered, the category you chose, and any Play Time attached to it. Above the list are running totals for today, this week, and this month, and the most recent sessions are listed underneath with the newest at the top.

Everything in this section lives behind one button.

Does time the metronome is held count as practice?

No. A session is the time the instrument was actually sounding. If a call arrives, or you switch away while in Mix, the transport holds and the practice clock holds with it, then both pick up together when you come back. A long interruption in the middle of a session no longer inflates its length, and if the Accelerator has split the session into work and play the held time is deducted from whichever side it fell on.

Do I have to press anything to save a session?

Press End Session, or Save & Finish where you see it, and the session is written. Sessions you abandon mid-climb are not recorded, which is deliberate. A log you can trust is worth more than a log that is generous.  NOTE: this can be changed if there is feedback. I want to encourage completion: do what you said. Plan the work. Work the plan. Feedback encouraged about this. Not everyone is wired the way I am. (OMG thank goodness)

Why does it ask for my name?

To put your name on your own practice log and nothing else. It is stored on your device, it is not sent anywhere, and no account is created. Leave it blank if you would rather not personalize this.

Where is my history actually stored?

On the device you are holding, in the browser's own storage. No server sees it unless you deliberately connect the sync described below. The practical consequence is worth understanding: clearing your browser data will delete your practice history, and so will a browser set to erase site data on quit. Export a copy, or connect the sync, or both.

Can I get my data out?

Yes, in two formats, and it is worth doing regularly. Export CSV gives you a spreadsheet file you can open anywhere and chart however you like. Export JSON gives you a complete and exact copy, and Import JSON reads one back in. The JSON file is the one to keep, because it is the one that can restore everything if you roam or switch devices.

08

Practice History and streaks

What is the calendar showing me?

One mark for every day, arranged by month, colored by what you practiced. A day with three categories in it shows three colors. A day you did not practice shows nothing. Tap a day to see the sessions it contains.

The streak sits above the month. Today is outlined, and its colors are the categories you practiced.

The point of the view is the pattern rather than any single day. Six weeks laid out at once shows you the shape of your practice: where the gaps fall, which day of the week you always lose, whether the good stretch you remember was three weeks or nine days.

How do I read one of the circles?

One circle is one day, and a full circle is one hour. The arcs fill clockwise in quarter turns, so each quarter is fifteen minutes and the colors are whatever categories you practiced, in the order you practiced them.

Past an hour the outline turns gold and a white number appears in the middle. That number is the hours for the day to one decimal, so five fifteen-minute sessions reads 1.3 and a long Sunday might read 4.5. It is there because a full circle is as much as the arcs can say: without a number, two hours and five hours would draw exactly alike.

Can I see what a day actually contained?

Tap any day that has already happened. A card opens with the day's circle, its totals, where the time went by category, and every session in order with the time you began, the tempo range it ran across, and how long it lasted.

Tap a day you did not play and it says so. Close it with the X, by tapping outside the card, or with the escape key.

A day opened. Totals, categories, and every session with its tempo range.

What are the lines under the calendar?

The month you are looking at, totaled. Hours for the month, how many days you played, and the average across those days. It follows whichever month is on screen, so paging back gives you last month rather than this one.

Under it, when there is any, is your play time: the minutes beyond the Accelerator target, counted apart from the rest.

Which day does a session count towards?

The day where you were when you played it. Each session records its local date and the time zone it was played in, so an evening session in Seattle stays on that evening, and a course in La Plata or a week in Pershore lands on the day you actually practiced rather than on whatever date it happened to be in Greenwich at the time. Sessions recorded before this was true keep their exact moment, and their day is worked out in whatever zone you are reading them from.

What is the streak?

The number of consecutive days up to today with at least one recorded session. Miss a day and it returns to zero. It is the same motivating mechanism Duolingo uses for language learners, and it works for the same slightly undignified reason: a number you do not want to lose will get you to pick up the instrument on the evening you had decided not to.

Treat it as a nudge rather than a judgment. A streak measures how many days in a row you showed up, and (of course) it says nothing about whether the work was any good.

09

Sync across devices

Why does my history not follow me between devices on its own?

Because it lives on each device rather than on a server. A browser has no way of knowing that the phone in your pocket and the laptop on the desk belong to the same person. Practice on the phone and the laptop knows nothing about it. Connecting the sync is what joins them.

How does the sync work?

Your practice log is stored in a private file inside a free GitHub account. GitHub is a service developers use to store code, and one of the things it offers is a private file store with an interface any app can use. This app uses that (for now). The file is yours, in your account, and I have no access to it.

You create a key in your GitHub settings, paste it into the sync field, and the app uses that key to read and write one private file. No password is shared with anyone. Save to cloud writes this device's history up. Load from cloud brings it down onto a new device. Turn on the automatic option and every completed session is saved up without your involvement.

Why GitHub and not an ordinary account with a password?

Because an ordinary account means a server holding your data and me holding your password. Both of those are liabilities for you and obligations for me, and neither is necessary to move a small file between two of your own devices. Your data sits in your account under your control, and I never see it. The cost of that choice is one afternoon of slightly technical setup, which is the (initial)_ trade-off I decided was worth making. I may revisit this and provide better auth in the future. Partially, this depends upon demand. Would this be useful for you? 

What happens if I practice on two devices before syncing?

Load from cloud on a device replaces what is on that device. Save from a device replaces what is in the cloud. The straightforward habit is to load when you arrive at a device and save when you leave it, and to leave the automatic option on so the second half happens for you.

My categories are named the same on both devices. Do they merge?

Yes. Categories travel with the log and are matched by name. Spell Scales the same way on the phone and the laptop and they are treated as one category. NOTE: I've chosen to populate the Tiny Orchestral Metronome with eight of my own practice categories that I'm using this year. You can delete all of these and provide your own, as useful. 

10

Solo and Mix

What is the Solo and Mix switch?

It decides whether the metronome owns the speaker or shares it, and each answer buys you one thing and costs you another. Solo keeps the click going when the screen turns off (auto-lock, for example), or when you switch to another app, or when the side mute switch is on, and the cost is that it takes the speaker for itself and mutes whatever else was playing. "Mix" mode lets the click play over a backing track, a podcast, a YouTube video - or anything else, and the cost is that it pauses when you switch away, and the side mute switch silences it. These are trade-offs. What is best for you? I don't know, you may need to experiment. 

Pauses rather than stops, and the difference matters. Nothing is torn down when the click goes quiet. Your tempo, bar count, category, accelerator step, and elapsed time all stay exactly where they were, and the click resumes in phase when you come back rather than catching up in a burst. If the phone refuses to hand the audio back on its own, an orange bar appears and the next tap anywhere resumes it. The same is true for incoming phone calls. Intention is to always PAUSE, the resume. 

What happens Solo Mix
Keeps clicking when the screen locks or you switch apps Yes No, it pauses
Other audio can play at the same time No, it is quieted Yes
Still sounds with the side mute switch on Yes No, it is silenced
Three behaviors, one switch. The phone ties them together and offers no way to have all three.

The limitation is based on phone architecture more than limitations of this app. A native iOS app can request both at once through a flag that Safari does not make available to web pages. 😬 Given a choice between the two, the switch is a reasonable trade-off. NOTE: I have not thoroughly tested this on Android devices. Or OSX. Or Windows. However, please share bugs, feature ideas, or issues you discover if you wish to help me improve this over time. 

Which one should I use?

Leave it on Solo for ordinary practice, where the phone is face down on the music stand and you want the click to survive the screen locking. Move it to Mix when you are playing along with or listening to something else while practicing: and keep the phone awake and in front of you while you do in this mode. It can help to change your lockscreen default to > 15m if you don't want interruptions from iOS to auto-pause your foreground practice.

If you ever find the metronome silent in Mix, check your iPhone side 'mute' switch before anything else. That is almost always the answer.

Moving the switch while the metronome is running produces a short break in the click, and that break is deliberate. Changing between the two settings asks the phone to change how it is using its speaker, and the phone will sometimes move the audio hardware to a different sample rate to suit. Doing that underneath a sound already in flight bends its pitch and unsettles the clock the beats are timed against. So the click stops, the setting changes in the silence, and the click resumes about a tenth of a second later. Your tempo, your bar position, your practice session and any Accelerator ramp all carry straight through the gap untouched.

Your choice is remembered between visits.

My metronome used to die when the screen locked. Is that fixed?

Yes, and the cause was not the audio setting. The metronome schedules its beats a little way ahead of time and tops that queue up on a timer. Phones deliberately slow those timers down to about once a second when the screen locks, so the queue emptied faster than it was refilled and the sound stopped. It now queues three seconds ahead whenever the page is hidden and drops back when you return, and a keepalive keeps the audio path open. The beats are still placed on the audio clock rather than on the timer, so nothing drifts.

A phone call came in and the metronome went silent for good. What now?

Tap the screen. A call takes the audio away and phones often refuse to give it back without a human touch. When that happens, the transport freezes rather than resetting, an orange bar appears saying the session is held, and the next tap anywhere resumes it. Your tempo, bar count, category, and elapsed time all survive the interruption.

This is the bar. It means nothing was lost. Tap and carry on.
11

Devices, offline, privacy

What do I need to run it?

A web browser. That covers iPhone, iPad, Android, Mac, Windows, and Linux. Nothing is installed and there is no store to visit. Open steveball.com/metronome and it runs.

Can I put it on my home screen like an app?

Yes, and it behaves better that way. On iPhone or iPad, open it in Safari, press Share, then Add to Home Screen. On Android, use the browser menu and Install or Add to Home screen. It then opens full screen with no browser bars, which is what you want on a music stand.

Does it work without an internet connection?

Yes, once you have opened it at least once. The app keeps a copy of itself on your device and falls back to that copy when the network is unavailable, so a practice room with no signal is fine. When you are online it asks the network first, which is how a new version reaches you.

Why is the whole thing a single file?

Because a single file cannot half-load. The dial, the sounds, the fonts, the logo, and every line of code live in one HTML document. There is nothing to fetch separately, nothing to break because one small file failed to arrive, and nothing to go missing when a server moves. It also means the entire instrument can be saved, copied, and archived by saving one page.

What do you collect about me?

Nothing. There is no analytics, no advertising, no tracking, and no account. Your name, your categories, and your practice log sit on your device. If you connect the sync, they also sit in a private file in your own GitHub account, and I have no access to it.

What does it cost?

Nothing. It is free to use. For now.

12

The iOS app

Is there going to be a real app?

Yes — it is here. The native iOS app, Accelerating Metronome, is finished and in TestFlight beta now, with its official App Store release on Friday, 7 August 2026. The web version continues exactly as it is, free, and it remains the version I developed first.

What does a native app get me that the browser cannot?

Chiefly, the things Safari refuses to hand to a web page. Solo and Mix become one setting instead of a choice, because a native app can request both at once. Audio survives interruptions without needing a tap. Lock screen controls, Apple Watch, notifications for a streak about to lapse, and audio routing to a specific interface all become possible. Timing on a phone is also simply steadier when the code is not sitting inside a browser.

Will it cost money?

The app may eventually support a paid tier for the advanced features, while the browser version stays free. The current idea is that everything you can do today you will still be able to do for nothing, and the deeper tools (customization, roaming) that only a native app can offer are what the paid tier is for. Exact pricing and the exact split are not decided and I would rather announce them once than guess at them now.

Will my practice history come with me?

Your history lives on your device. The iOS app keeps your practice log, categories, and settings in its own on-device storage, and you can export the whole log as JSON at any time to move it or keep a backup. Keep a copy.

Is my data private? What does the iOS app collect?

It collects nothing, and it keeps your data on your iPhone. Unlike the web version, the iOS app does not use GitHub or any cloud service, and it has no server, no account, and no sign-in — nothing you enter is sent anywhere by the app. There is no analytics, advertising, or tracking. The only copy that ever leaves the phone is the one iOS folds into your standard, end-to-end encrypted iCloud backup under your Apple ID, exactly as it does for every app; that backup is Apple's and I have no access to it. Full details are in Privacy & data.

13

Privacy & data

This is the privacy policy for the Accelerating Metronome iOS app and the Tiny Orchestral Metronome web app. Last updated 4 August 2026. In one line: the app collects nothing about you and keeps your practice data on your own device.

What data does the app collect?

None. The Accelerating Metronome iOS app collects no personal data whatsoever. There is no account, no sign-in, no analytics, no advertising, no tracking, no third-party SDKs, and nothing is sold or shared. This matches Apple's "Data Not Collected" disclosure shown on the App Store product page.

Where is my practice data stored?

On your device, and nowhere else by the app. Your practice history, categories, session names, and settings are saved in the app's private on-device storage. The iOS app does not use GitHub or any other cloud service, and it has no server of its own; nothing you enter is transmitted off the device by the app.

What about iCloud and my Apple ID?

The app never reads or writes your Apple ID. Because your data lives in the app's on-device storage, iOS may include it in your standard, end-to-end encrypted iCloud device backup, exactly as it does for every app you install. That backup is operated by Apple under your Apple ID and Apple's privacy terms; the developer has no access to it and receives none of that data.

Does the app use my microphone, location, contacts, or other sensors?

No. The app plays audio and, optionally, uses the Taptic Engine for haptic feedback on the beat. It does not request or access the microphone, camera, location, contacts, photos, health data, or any other personal information.

Children's privacy

Because the app collects no personal information from anyone, it collects none from children, and it does not knowingly gather data from users under 13. It is safe for use by all ages.

Can I delete my data?

Entirely, and it is under your control. Your data is on your device, so deleting the app removes it. You can also export your practice log as JSON at any time to keep your own copy first.

Changes and contact

If this policy changes, the updated version is posted here with a new date. Questions about privacy can be sent through steveball.com. Publisher: Steve Ball, Ballistic Music, Seattle, Washington.
